overview.text: The Burning or Unburnt Bush icon connects the vision of Moses with the Church’s confession of the Incarnation. The OCA explains both an older narrative form and a later star-shaped composition.

blocks.text: This early-eighteenth-century example depicts Moses beside the bush, with the Mother of God and Child above. It illustrates the narrative form of the subject. The source record identifies an old icon; the photograph is used complete and unchanged.

blocks.text: The OCA names the bush that burns without being consumed as an Old Testament prefiguration of the Virgin’s childbearing. It also describes a later composition combining red and green quadrangles, prophetic scenes, angels, and the central Mother and Child. That description should be read as a type with variants, rather than a list of features visible in every example.

blocks.title: Exodus 3:1–6
blocks.text:
Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian: and he led the flock to the backside of the desert, and came to the mountain of God, even to Horeb.

And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.

And Moses said, I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.

And when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him out of the midst of the bush, and said, Moses, Moses. And he said, Here am I.

And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.

Moreover he said, I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. And Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look upon God.
